hints: Notice the wording immediately after he opens his parachute and that he is already falling vertically downwards fast.
Recall drag force acts opposite to velocity, so opening the large parachute suddenly makes upward air resistance much larger than weight.
Connect an upward resultant force on a downward-moving mass to deceleration: the direction of motion stays the same while the speed drops.
walkthrough: Identify the starting state: the skydiver has a large velocity directed vertically downwards just before the parachute opens.
State the force change: opening the parachute greatly increases effective area, so upward drag $F_{drag}$ suddenly becomes greater than downward weight $W$.
Find the resultant: $F_{net} = F_{drag} - W$ acts upwards, so by $F = ma$ the acceleration $a$ is upwards.
Apply acceleration to velocity: velocity is still downwards, but acceleration is upwards, so the change in velocity $\Delta v = a \Delta t$ is upwards and subtracts from the downward motion.
Conclude the effect: the skydiver continues moving downwards for now but slows down, so direction is downwards and magnitude decreases. This is option A.

options.A: Velocity stays downwards because motion cannot reverse instantly, and speed decreases because upward drag now exceeds weight giving upward acceleration.
options.B: Direction downwards is correct but magnitude cannot increase because the larger drag produces an upward resultant force that decelerates the fall.
options.C: Magnitude decreasing is correct but direction cannot become upwards immediately - the skydiver is still moving down and only slows down.
options.D: Direction cannot switch to upwards and speed cannot increase - the parachute creates large upward drag that opposes the downward motion.
